terms.meaning: a line in a code file that pulls in code written in another file
a level in the app's structure, such as data access, business logic, or screens, where lower levels must not depend on higher ones
code used by many parts of the app, such as permissions or AI helpers, that enters through one agreed door

sections.name: File setup, LAYERS, RANK
sections.title: Setup and layer order
sections.what: Declares the file's tools and the ordered list of layers, plus a rank for each layer that says which ones may depend on which. This is the rulebook the other sections check against.
sections.why: Keeps the layer order in one place so every rule reads from the same ranking.
sections.watch_out: If a new layer is added to the app, it must be added here or the check will not know where it sits.

sections.name: Violation
sections.title: Violation record shape
sections.what: Defines what one problem report looks like: the file, the import text, and the message.
sections.why: Gives every failure the same shape so reports can be printed or sorted the same way.

sections.name: listFiles
sections.title: Finding all code files
sections.what: Walks through every folder under the source root and collects TypeScript files, skipping type-declaration files.
sections.why: The check needs the full list of files to inspect, and it skips declaration files because they hold no runtime imports to judge.
sections.watch_out: Only files ending in the three recognised TypeScript extensions are checked, so a new file type would be skipped silently.

sections.name: target
sections.title: Resolving where an import points
sections.what: Turns an import text into a path relative to the source root, or returns nothing for outside packages. It handles the project's @ alias and relative paths.
sections.why: The rules compare locations, so every import has to be converted to a comparable location first.
sections.watch_out: Only the @ alias and dot-relative paths are understood; any other custom alias will be treated as an outside package.

sections.name: domainLayer
sections.title: Reading a domain's area and layer
sections.what: Given a path inside the domain folder, works out which business area it belongs to and which layer it sits in. Returns nothing for paths outside that structure.
sections.why: The layer rules only apply to files inside the domain folders, so this decides whether a file is covered.
sections.watch_out: A folder that does not match the expected area and layer naming pattern is quietly excluded from every layer rule.

sections.name: ENGINE_ALLOWED_PACKAGES
sections.title: Engine package allowance list
sections.what: Holds the list of outside packages the pure engine is allowed to import, and a pattern that recognises database modules.
sections.why: The engine must stay free of input and output code, so the allowance list is the only exception path and the database pattern is the thing it must not reach.
sections.watch_out: The allowance list is currently empty, so adding any outside package to the engine will fail the check until the list is updated.

sections.name: checkFile
sections.title: Checking one file's imports
sections.what: Reads one file's text, finds each import, and applies the rules: engine purity, no database in the UI, no route code or cross-cutting code direct from domains, no upward layer imports, and no reaching into another domain's repository or config.
sections.why: This is where each architecture rule actually lives, so it is the place to change when the rules change.
sections.watch_out: The rules use exact path prefixes, so renaming a folder like the engine or the providers folder will silently disable the matching rule.

sections.name: checkTree
sections.title: Checking the whole source tree
sections.what: Runs the single-file check on every file found under the source root and gathers all violations into one list.
sections.why: This is the entry point that a test runner calls to check the whole codebase at once.

summary: A structural check that reads every source file and reports imports that break the agreed layer order, with a fix hint for each break.
purpose: Keeps the code organised so that lower, more basic layers never depend on higher, more visible ones, and so the pure engine stays free of database and framework code.
why: Without this check, a developer could quietly import a database helper into a screen or a route handler into core logic, and the app would still run while getting harder to change.
how: It lists all non-test TypeScript files under the source root, reads each one, and finds every import, export-from, dynamic import and require. Each import is resolved to a path inside the source tree or marked as an outside package. It then applies four rules: the engine may only import engine code or approved packages, the UI may not touch database modules, domains may not reach into route code or cross-cutting code directly, and a domain may not import a higher layer or another domain's repository or config. Every break becomes a violation with a message that says how to fix it.
inputs: A source root folder path. The function checkTree reads every file under it; checkFile can also be given one file's path and text.
outputs: A list of violations. Each violation has the file path, the import text that caused it, and a plain message explaining the fix.
risks: The check uses pattern matching rather than a full code parser, so unusual import styles or multi-line edge cases could be missed or misread. The allowed-package list for the engine is currently empty, which means the engine may not import any outside package at all.
debug: If the check fails, read the message: it names the file and the import. If a valid import is flagged, check the layer order in the layer list and the rank table. If the check misses something, test a sample import against the import pattern. If it fails on a file that is not in the source tree, check the source root that was passed in.
